newsitem.title: TANZANIA: Tanzanian minister says economy on way up.
newsitem.headline: Tanzanian minister says economy on way up.

text.p: Tanzania's finance minister says punishing economic reforms at the behest of the International Monetary Fund and World Bank were beginning to show results for the economy.
Daniel Yona told Reuters that inflation was on a downward path and official corruption was diminishing as privatisation gathered pace.

Tanzania's gross domestic product growth is forecast at 4.5 percent in 1997 from 4.0 percent in 1996, according to government figures. Yona queried the statistical accuracy of that figure and diplomats working at leading financial institutions have said that growth was at least a point higher.
Yona said Tanzania's annualised inflation reached 13.8 percent in February from 14 percent in January and he was hopeful it would fall to a single-digit level this year.

"I'm tempted to say by July this year we'll hit 10 (percent)," he said, adding that tight fiscal policy would stay in force to keep inflationary pressure down. In January 1996, annual inflation was at 25 percent.

Asked what progress the government was making in overhauling its much-criticised taxation policy, Yona said a government- commissioned report into tax policy should be completed within the next week and held several surprises.
While declining to give specific details of change, the minister said the new tax policy to be announced in the June budget would be "investor friendly and taxpayer friendly."
Yona said Tanzania's new tax policy would put the country on a competitive level with neighbouring Kenya and Uganda and would act as an incentive to attract foreign and domestic investors.

"The aim is to bring them to a level where they will be competitive in the domestic and external market. We are revising our tax regime so we have fewer taxes, stable taxes. Some (taxes) are too high and too many -- in the hotel industry.
Yona acknowledged complaints by foreign businesses of excessive bureaucracy. He said it would take time to eradicate "but attitudes are changing".
He said the government was also stongly committed to fighting corruption and incidents of official corruption would diminish as the state continued on its privatisation programme.
Responding to criticisms that Tanzania's privatisation programme was going too slowly, Yona said of the 400 ailing state assets in 1992, about 150 had already been sold off.

Of that 150, some 30 state enterprises were completely bankrupt and selling them off presented some difficulties, Yona said: "Believe me, it's not always easy to sell these institutions. It's like taking a thin cow to the market."
